messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Leilani was twenty years old when the stalking began. She worked as an auditor at a mid-sized firm in the city, and during her first few months on the job, she caught the attention of a colleague whose interest quickly curdled into obsession. He would appear outside her cubicle at odd hours, leave notes on her desk with details about her lunch breaks, and follow her to the train station each evening. The police were called, but the behavior only turned more menacing—phone calls at night, a tracking device under her car, a message that read *I know where you live*. After six weeks of this, he was arrested, but Leilani’s sense of safety had already collapsed.

In the months that followed, she came to believe that the world had fundamentally changed. Every street corner felt like a potential hiding place, every stranger’s glance a threat. She told herself that her life had been destroyed by what happened—that the person she used to be, the one who walked home without checking over her shoulder, was gone for good. That belief hollowed her out. She began to feel that she had to be on guard all the time, scanning doorways, rehearsing escape routes, her body wired even in her own apartment. And because the world felt so dangerous, she started to withdraw. She avoided going out after work, cancelled plans with friends, and eventually stopped leaving her apartment except for the bare minimum—the grocery store at six in the morning when the aisles were empty. She also avoided any situation that might make her feel happy or hopeful, as if the faintest spark of ease would invite disaster. A compliment, a funny video, the offer of a coffee from a coworker—she turned them all away, convinced that relaxing her vigilance was a betrayal of what she now knew about the world.

The avoidance grew into something darker. Leilani began telling herself that she deserved to suffer for what happened. It started as a quiet thought—*you should have seen it coming, you should have been smarter*—and hardened into a daily ritual of self-punishment. She would replay the moments before the stalking escalated and blame herself for not recognizing the signs. The thought comforted her in a twisted way: if it was her fault, then maybe she could learn to avoid it next time. But the comfort never lasted. Instead, she found herself punishing herself for small lapses—for sleeping through an alarm, for eating a piece of chocolate, for laughing at a colleague’s joke. Pleasure felt dangerous, and suffering felt just.

At work, her performance began to slip. Auditing demands meticulous attention, but Leilani struggled to concentrate when every sound—a door opening, a phone ringing—sent her into a spiral of hypervigilance. She requested to work from home, but her supervisor noticed the drop in productivity and asked her to take a leave of absence. The isolation deepened. She stopped responding to messages from her family, who lived in a different state. She had no partner; she could not imagine letting anyone close enough to touch her, because touch meant vulnerability, and vulnerability had become unthinkable.

What finally brought her to therapy was the recognition that she could no longer go on this way—not because she wanted to feel better, but because her body was beginning to fail her: headaches, insomnia, a constant tightness in her chest that no amount of staying home could soothe. She walked into the clinic with her hands clenched in her lap, scanning the waiting room as if the stalker might be sitting in the chair beside her. When asked what she hoped for, she shook her head. She was certain that her life had been destroyed, but she was even more afraid that trying to rebuild it would only prove how thoroughly she deserved to suffer.
